%1$s is not a valid network address for /%2$d. The actual network starts at %3$s. Cloud providers like Azure require the exact network address in subnet definitions.

The network address is the first address in a subnet, with all host bits set to 0. It identifies the subnet itself and cannot be assigned to any device. Example: in 192.168.1.0/24 the network address is 192.168.1.0.

The broadcast address is the last address in a subnet, with all host bits set to 1. Packets sent here are delivered to every device in the subnet. Example: in 192.168.1.0/24 the broadcast is 192.168.1.255.
The first usable IP address — one above the network address. This is the lowest address you can assign to a device.
The last usable IP address — one below the broadcast address. This is the highest address you can assign to a device.
The count of addresses that can be assigned to devices. Always (2^host_bits − 2) because the network and broadcast addresses are reserved.
The wildcard mask is the bitwise inverse of the subnet mask. Bits set to 1 are "don\'t care" bits. Used in ACLs and OSPF configurations.
Classless Inter-Domain Routing notation combines an IP address with a prefix length (the number of network bits). Example: 192.168.1.0/24 means 24 network bits and 8 host bits.
A legacy classification of IPv4 ranges before CIDR replaced it. Class A covers 0–127, B covers 128–191, C covers 192–223. Class D is multicast, E is reserved.
Whether the address falls within RFC 1918 private ranges (10.x, 172.16–31.x, 192.168.x) or is publicly routable on the internet.

Every device on a network can be asked "are you there?" using a tiny message called an ICMP Echo Request — informally, a "ping." The target replies immediately if it\'s reachable. The time between sending the request and receiving the reply is the round-trip time (RTT), which tells you both whether a host is alive and how far away it is, network-wise.
Checks whether a host is reachable and measures round-trip time (RTT). The app resolves a hostname once, tries ICMP echo, and falls back to Android reachability when the ICMP socket is unavailable.

string-array.name: help_ping_params_bullets
string-array.item: Count — number of ping packets to send.
Timeout — how long to wait for each reply before marking it lost.
Advanced — choose payload size (0–1,472 bytes), TTL (1–255), and interval (100–10,000 ms).
Continuous — pings indefinitely until you stop it manually.

string-array.name: help_ping_results_bullets
string-array.item: Min / Avg / Max — the fastest, typical, and slowest round-trip times seen.
Jitter — how much RTT varies between pings; high jitter means an unstable connection, even if the average looks fine.
Packet loss — the percentage of pings that got no reply; anything above 0%% suggests congestion or a firewall dropping packets.
Unreachable — the network explicitly rejected the probe before the timeout; this is different from a silent timeout.

resources.string: Every packet carries a small "hop counter" (TTL, or Time To Live) that starts at a number and drops by 1 at every router it passes through. When a router sees the counter hit 0, it discards the packet and sends back a "time exceeded" message — revealing itself. Traceroute exploits this: it sends packets with the counter set to 1, then 2, then 3 and so on, so each router along the path replies in turn, mapping the route your data takes, hop by hop.
Discovers the path packets take from your device to a destination by incrementing the IP TTL and recording each router that responds.

string-array.name: help_traceroute_params_bullets
string-array.item: Max hops — the highest hop count to try before giving up.
Probe protocol — ICMP is more likely to get a reply; UDP mimics the traditional traceroute tool.
Probes per hop — how many probes to send at each hop count, to average out inconsistent replies.

string-array.name: help_traceroute_results_bullets
string-array.item: Each row is one router hop along the path.
\'*\' means that router didn\'t respond — common with routers configured to ignore these probes, not necessarily a problem.
Journey Intelligence — for public IPs, shows geographic location, RTT analysis, and which ISP owns that hop.

resources.string: An IP address gets your data to the right device — like a street address gets mail to the right building. A port number then gets it to the right service running on that device — like an apartment number inside the building. A web server usually listens on port 80 or 443, a mail server on 25, and so on; scanning a range of ports tells you which of these "apartments" have someone answering.
Attempts TCP connections to a range of ports on a host to determine which are open, closed, or filtered. Useful for auditing what services are exposed.

string-array.name: help_portscan_params_bullets
string-array.item: Port range — use a preset (Common, Web, All) or enter a custom range.
Timeout — how long to wait for each port before giving up.
Concurrency — how many ports to check at the same time.

string-array.name: help_portscan_results_bullets
string-array.item: Open — something answered; a service is listening on that port.
Closed — the port actively refused the connection; nothing is listening there.
Filtered — no response at all within the timeout, typically because a firewall is silently blocking it.
Banners — when available, the service\'s own self-identification text (e.g. server name/version).

resources.string: Devices on your home or office network share a private range of addresses, like 192.168.1.1 through 192.168.1.254. That range is written in CIDR notation as 192.168.1.0/24, where the "/24" says how many addresses are included. The scanner uses ICMP, TCP, and optional local name probes to find devices that answer even when ordinary ping is blocked.

Checks every address in a subnet with ICMP and TCP, then uses NetBIOS or mDNS names as additional presence evidence. Responsive hosts are enriched with hostnames, open ports, and a best-effort ARP MAC/vendor lookup.

string-array.name: help_lan_params_bullets
string-array.item: Subnet (CIDR) — e.g. 192.168.1.0/24; tap \'Detect\' to auto-fill your current subnet.
Timeout — how long to wait for each host to respond.
Concurrency — how many hosts to probe at the same time.

string-array.name: help_lan_results_bullets
string-array.item: Discovery chips explain whether ICMP, TCP, NetBIOS, mDNS, or reverse DNS contributed to the result.
MAC addresses may be unavailable on Android 10 and later because apps cannot read the ARP cache.
The gateway comes from the active network default route. Tap a host for details or Scan ports.

resources.string: Every website has a numeric address (like 142.250.80.14) that computers use to find it, but people use names instead (like google.com). DNS is the internet\'s phone book: it translates the name you type into the number your device actually connects to. A record type just tells the phone book which kind of information you want back — an address, a mail server, ownership proof, and so on.
Queries a DNS server for records associated with a domain or IP address. Supports A, AAAA, MX, TXT, CNAME, NS, SOA, PTR, SRV, and more.

string-array.name: help_dns_params_bullets
string-array.item: Domain — the hostname or IP to query.

Record type — A/AAAA return the IP address; MX returns the mail server that handles email for the domain; TXT holds arbitrary text, often used to prove domain ownership; CNAME is an alias pointing to another name; NS lists the servers authoritative for the domain; SOA holds zone administration info; PTR reverse-resolves an IP back to a hostname; SRV points to the host/port for a specific service.
DNS server — choose System, Google, Cloudflare, OpenDNS, Quad9, or enter a custom resolver IP.

string-array.name: help_dns_results_bullets
string-array.item: TTL (time-to-live) is in seconds — it tells other resolvers and browsers how long they\'re allowed to cache this answer before asking again.
The raw response tab shows the full DNS wire-format response.
RCODE, flags, Authority, Additional, and the actual server used explain negative answers and resolver behaviour.
Private DNS is reported when Android exposes it; System DNS is never silently replaced by another resolver.
Use PTR lookups to reverse-resolve an IP address to a hostname.

resources.string: Wi-Fi radios talk over slices of radio frequency called channels, similar to how radio stations each get their own frequency so they don\'t talk over each other. Every network you see is a named group (SSID) that can be broadcast by one or more physical radios, each with its own hardware address (BSSID) — a mesh system or dual-band router shows up as one SSID but several BSSIDs. 2.4 GHz channels travel further through walls but there are only 3 that don\'t overlap, so they get crowded; 5 GHz and 6 GHz have far more non-overlapping channels and are faster, at the cost of shorter range.

Triggers a platform Wi-Fi scan, groups nearby access points by network (SSID), and displays channel utilisation on a spectrum chart. Location Services and the Android Wi-Fi scan permissions are required; your location is not recorded or sent.

string-array.name: help_wifi_params_bullets
string-array.item: Scan — request a fresh platform scan.
Auto-refresh — choose Off, 15, 30, or 60 seconds.
If Android throttles a request, the screen shows the cached result age.
Location Services must be enabled for Android to return scan results.
Band filter — show only 2.4 GHz, 5 GHz, or 6 GHz networks.
Sort — order by signal strength, channel, or SSID.

string-array.name: help_wifi_results_bullets
string-array.item: The spectrum chart shows AP signal curves by frequency.
Overlapping curves mean channel congestion — multiple networks competing for the same slice of spectrum.
The Best Channel callout recommends the least-congested 2.4 GHz channel.
Tap a network to expand per-BSSID details; tap an AP row for full connection detail.

resources.string: Switches and routers understand SNMP (Simple Network Management Protocol), a standard way for network gear to report its status and configuration — like each device having its own public status page a tool can read. This app asks one device "who are you connected to?", then asks each of those neighbours the same question, building a map hop by hop, the way you\'d trace a chain of introductions at a party. The result is a picture of how your switches and routers are physically wired together.
Uses SNMP to query a seed switch or router and discover its neighbours, building an interactive topology graph of your network infrastructure.

string-array.name: help_topology_params_bullets
string-array.item: Target IP — the IP of the first device to query, the starting point for the map.
SNMP version — v1, v2c, or v3; v3 adds authentication and encryption the older versions lack.
Community string — a shared password required for v1/v2c (default is \'public\', a notoriously insecure default many devices still ship with — change it if you can).
SNMP v3 privacy requires authentication first; auth and privacy passwords are kept in memory for the scan and are never logged.
Max hops — how many device-to-device introductions to follow before stopping.

string-array.name: help_topology_results_bullets
string-array.item: Nodes represent discovered devices; lines represent the SNMP-reported links between them.
Pinch to zoom, drag to pan around the graph.
Tap a node to view its system information, interfaces, VLANs, and neighbours.
Useful for mapping an office network, spotting unexpected devices, or documenting infrastructure before troubleshooting a connectivity issue.

resources.string: What is TLS, and why does the certificate chain matter?

TLS (the "S" in HTTPS) scrambles traffic between your device and a server so anyone else on the network can\'t read it. But encryption alone doesn\'t prove who you\'re talking to — that\'s what certificates are for: a certificate is like an ID card proving "this server really is example.com," signed by a trusted authority. The chain (leaf → intermediate → root) is the paper trail of who vouched for whom, ending at a small set of root authorities your device already trusts by default.
Opens a TLS connection to a host and retrieves the full certificate chain, including expired, self-signed, or untrusted certificates that a browser would normally hide.

string-array.name: help_tls_params_bullets
string-array.item: Host — the domain name or IP to connect to.
Port — the TLS port (default 443 for HTTPS; 8443, 993, 465 are common alternatives).

string-array.name: help_tls_results_bullets
string-array.item: The connection card shows the TLS version, cipher suite, and handshake time.
Each certificate in the chain (leaf, intermediate, root) expands to show subject, issuer, validity dates, SANs, and the SHA-256 fingerprint.
A red badge means expired — the site\'s ID card is out of date and your connection can\'t be fully verified, similar to a browser warning page.

resources.string: WHOIS is a public registry of who owns a domain name or block of IP addresses and since when — like checking a property deed. Every domain and IP range has an owner on record somewhere, and WHOIS servers let anyone look that record up.
Queries WHOIS servers to retrieve registration information for a domain name, IP address, or Autonomous System Number (ASN).

string-array.name: help_whois_params_bullets
string-array.item: Domain — e.g. example.com.
IP address — e.g. 8.8.8.8.

ASN — e.g. AS15169; an Autonomous System Number identifies a large network or organization (typically an ISP) that controls a block of addresses and announces routes for them — one level above individual IP ranges.
Use the quick-fill chips to insert an example of each type.

string-array.name: help_whois_results_bullets
string-array.item: For domains: registrant, registration/expiry dates, name servers, and status codes — handy for checking if a domain is about to expire or investigating who\'s behind a site.
For IPs: the network range, owning organisation, and country — useful for finding the ISP or hosting provider behind an address.
The Raw section shows the unprocessed WHOIS server response.

resources.string: What happens when you "visit" a URL?

When you request a URL, your device opens a connection to a server and sends a small text message describing what you want — the method, headers, maybe a body. The server replies with a status code, its own headers, and the content. This tool lets you send that request directly and inspect the entire exchange, including security-related response headers browsers check automatically but rarely show you.
Sends an HTTP or HTTPS request to a URL and displays the full response including status, headers, body, redirect chain, and a security header analysis.

string-array.name: help_httprobe_params_bullets
string-array.item: URL — the full address including https://
Method — GET, POST, PUT, PATCH, DELETE, HEAD, OPTIONS.
Custom headers — add Authorization, Accept, Content-Type, etc.
Request body — JSON or other payload for POST/PUT.
Follow redirects — automatically follow 3xx responses.

string-array.name: help_httprobe_results_bullets
string-array.item: Overview — status code, response time, and final URL after redirects.
Headers — every request and response header.
Body — the response body, with size and truncation shown if applicable.
Security — see below.

string-array.name: help_httprobe_security_bullets
string-array.item: HSTS — forces browsers to always use the encrypted (https) version of this site.
CSP — restricts which scripts and resources a page may load, blocking many injection attacks.
X-Frame-Options — stops other sites from embedding this page in a hidden frame to trick users into clicking it (clickjacking).
X-Content-Type-Options — stops browsers from guessing a file\'s type in a way attackers can exploit.
Referrer-Policy — controls how much of the current URL leaks to sites you click through to.
Permissions-Policy — restricts which browser features (camera, mic, location) a page can use.
Cross-Origin-Opener-Policy — isolates this tab from being manipulated by a malicious page it opened or was opened by.
Cross-Origin-Embedder-Policy — requires cross-origin resources to explicitly opt in before this page can use them, closing another cross-tab attack path.
Server — whether the response reveals software/version info attackers could use to look up known vulnerabilities.

resources.string: An IP address has two parts: a network part shared by every device on that local network, and a host part unique to each device — like a street name shared by a block of houses and a house number unique to each one. The subnet mask (the "/24" in CIDR notation) says how many bits belong to each part, which determines how many devices fit and where one network\'s addresses end and the next begins. Splitting a large network into smaller subnets is how organizations keep traffic organized, secure, and easier to manage.
Calculates network details from a CIDR notation or dot-decimal mask input, and can find the smallest subnet that covers a given IP range.

string-array.name: help_subnet_params_bullets
string-array.item: CIDR/Mask mode — enter an address like 192.168.1.0/24 or 10.0.0.0/255.255.0.0.
IP Range mode — enter the smallest and largest IPs you need; the tool finds the tightest enclosing subnet.

string-array.name: help_subnet_results_bullets
string-array.item: Network and broadcast addresses, first/last usable hosts, and usable host count.
Binary Breakdown — shows exactly which bits are network vs host bits.
Notation Equivalents — CIDR, dot-decimal, wildcard, hex, and binary representations.
Tap the \'i\' icons for field-level explanations.

resources.string: Regular DNS relies on a central server to look up names. mDNS (also called Bonjour or Zeroconf) skips that: devices on your local network announce themselves by shouting their name and services to a special multicast address that every listening device on the network receives at once, and everyone else just listens for those announcements. That\'s how a printer or speaker can be found automatically without you ever typing its address.
Listens for multicast DNS (mDNS / Bonjour / Zeroconf) announcements on your local network to discover services like printers, media servers, smart home devices, and developer tools.

string-array.name: help_mdns_params_bullets
string-array.item: Scan — starts an 8-second discovery window; run it multiple times to catch devices that announce infrequently.
Stop — end the current scan early.
Reset — clear all results.

string-array.name: help_mdns_results_bullets
string-array.item: Services are grouped by type (e.g. _http._tcp, _airplay._tcp).
Tap a group to expand it and see individual service instances.
Each instance shows its hostname, IP address, port, and any TXT record properties.

resources.string: Latency vs. bandwidth — what\'s actually being measured?

Latency is how long it takes a single small message to get a reply — it matters for anything interactive, like gaming or video calls. Bandwidth (or throughput) is how much data can flow per second once a connection gets going — it matters for downloads and streaming quality. Most home internet plans are asymmetric, provisioned for much faster downloads than uploads, since most everyday usage is downloading or streaming rather than sending large amounts of data out.
Measures your connection\'s latency, download speed, and upload speed by exchanging data with Cloudflare\'s speed test service (speed.cloudflare.com).
The test runs each phase in sequence automatically.

string-array.name: help_speedtest_phases_bullets
string-array.item: Latency — sends small requests to measure round-trip time and jitter.
Download — downloads progressively larger payloads and records throughput.
Upload — uploads data to measure upload speed.

string-array.name: help_speedtest_results_bullets
string-array.item: Average speed — the sustained throughput across the full phase.
Peak speed — the highest burst observed.
The throughput chart shows speed over time — a flat line suggests a bandwidth cap; a jagged line suggests network instability.

resources.string: Measure download, upload speed and latency against Cloudflare\'s global network
Test traffic is sent to and measured by Cloudflare\'s speed.cloudflare.com service. Net Swiss Knife is not affiliated with, sponsored by, or endorsed by Cloudflare, Inc.
Measures latency, download, and upload speed in sequence
Hostname or IP cannot contain spaces
Wake sleeping devices with a magic packet
Port 9 (discard) is the convention; some devices use 7
Delivery is fire-and-forget: the target machine must have Wake-on-LAN enabled in its firmware/OS and be on the same network.

Wake-on-LAN (WOL) wakes a powered-down or sleeping computer by sending a special UDP "magic packet" containing its MAC address repeated 16 times. The network card listens for this pattern even while the machine sleeps.

Use the LAN Scanner tool to discover devices and their MAC addresses while they are awake, or check the device\'s network settings. Formats AA:BB:CC:DD:EE:FF, AA-BB-CC-DD-EE-FF, AABB.CCDD.EEFF and AABBCCDDEEFF are all accepted.
Wake-on-LAN must be enabled in the target\'s BIOS/UEFI and operating system network adapter settings. Wired Ethernet is most reliable; Wi-Fi wake (WoWLAN) support varies by hardware.

The default 255.255.255.255 broadcasts to the whole local network. For a specific subnet use its directed broadcast address (e.g. 192.168.1.255). Port 9 is conventional; port 7 is a common alternative.
Enter a valid IPv4 or IPv6 address
